speaker_role: student/former applicant (speaks from personal high school experience; not a counselor or admissions officer)
key_insights: Argues that once GPA and test scores are similarly strong across applicants, distinctive extracurricular activities become the differentiator admissions officers remember
Claims colleges value activities that show a student could contribute to campus life beyond academics (e.g., research groups, arts, athletics) so the student body isn't uniformly just 'smart'
Argues an extracurricular is more meaningful if the student achieved some form of external recognition or measurable progress in it, rather than just participating informally

Illustrates this with his own participation in a defunct College Board program (Young Epidemiology Scholars), informally searching program alumni names alongside university names to suggest many went on to attend selective schools
Suggests his own participation in this now-discontinued program was a distinguishing element of his own application
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states the Young Epidemiology Scholars program (via the College Board) held its last cohort in April 2011; he participated in the second-to-last year, having graduated high school in 2010
Speaker informally counts search-engine 'hits' pairing program alumni names with schools like Yale, Harvard, Columbia, Duke, and Brown as evidence many went to selective schools
notable_or_distinctive: The methodology used to support the central claim (manually counting how many search-engine hits pair alumni names with elite school names) is unusually weak evidence for the claim being made.
reliability_notes: Older video (published about a decade ago per the manifest) discussing a college program that no longer exists (discontinued in 2011); the core evidentiary method (informal name/school search-hit counting) is anecdotal and not a reliable way to establish that the activity caused admissions success.
